PAPER: Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11002-025-09799-x ORIGINAL RESEARCH True pricing – guiding consumers within a new pricing paradigm Anne O. Peschel1 · Michiel C. J. Bliemer2 · John Thøgersen1 Received: 23 April 2025 / Accepted: 5 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract True pricing is an innovative pricing approach, internalizing external costs in the final selling price, thereby increasing prices in general and more the more unsustain- able offerings are. It is important to understand how to best communicate true prices at the point of sale, to guide consumers in their decision-making. Here, we present the results of a large-scale survey experiment with 1400 Dutch and Danish consum- ers, investigating the effect of the true price presentation format (absolute, relative or no information) on consumers’ choices. Our results show that importance of price differs depending on the presentation format. Further, consumers with a stronger belief in the price-quality relationship are more prone to accept higher true prices (i.e., less sustainable options), which is reversed by consumers’ understanding of true pricing. We contribute to the marketing literature on price presentation format as well as true pricing and provide managerial guidance on implementing true price communication. Keywords True pricing · Labeling · Sustainability · Organic · Food 1 Introduction During their True Cost (“Wahre Kosten”) campaign week, German retailer Penny charged up to 94% more for their private label cheese and up to 88% more for sausages (Penny, 2024). The difference between regular selling price and true price in products sold was donated to a German initiative for sustainable farming. Dutch retailer Albert Heijn ran a similar campaign charging true prices for coffee (True Price, 2024). Here, the difference between regular price and true price in * Anne O. Both campaigns were heavily covered in the media and received mixed responses from praising the effort made in the sustainability domain to accusations of greenwash- ing. The media focus was primarily on the higher prices that consumers faced and that consumers’ willingness to pay true prices was rather low (Stein et al., 2024). However, the idea behind true cost accounting (TCA) is a slightly different one. It builds on the assumption that the current food system is unsustainable. To secure safe and affordable food for future generations, a transition towards a more sustainable food system is needed (Willett et al., 2019). While a food sys- tem has many actors, the marketplaces, such as the retail setting, may support a system transition as this is where consumers make their choices, among the options provided by the retailer. In terms of TCA, it is important to note that the regular selling price consumers pay at the retail level does not account for the damage that current production practices cause to the environment, human health, the living conditions of communities in developing countries, and others. Current estimates suggest that the cost of externalities is up to twice the market value of food production (Hendriks et al., 2023). If the costs of greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity loss, diseases, or unfair wages would be incorporated into the selling price, more sustainable products would be relatively less expensive, while unsus- tainable products would increase substantially in price (Michalke et al., 2022). Consequently, under a true pricing paradigm (which implements true costs into selling prices), consumers might not have to pay higher prices if they choose to purchase more sustainably. True pricing therefore offers incentives to shift con- sumers’ choices to more sustainable options. Few studies have investigated true pricing from a marketing perspective. The question we pose in this paper is how marketers can guide consumers in making choices under this new true pricing paradigm. To inform theory and marketing prac- titioners on how to most effectively present these types of price premiums to con- sumers, our main focus is on the presentation format of the hidden cost of prod- ucts. Taufik et al. (2023) highlight the importance of trust in the retailer and in true price calculations. Wilken et al. (2024) showed that true pricing information can increase the perception of prices as fair, which in turn can increase the acceptance of higher true prices, as suggested by more established contributions in the pric- ing literature (Bolton & Alba, 2006; Bolton et al., 2003). However, increasing the acceptance of higher true prices might not be sufficient to make choices more sus- tainable. With many consumers having internalized a price-quality schema where higher prices mean higher quality (Lichtenstein et al., 1993; Völckner & Hofmann, 2007), a higher true price might be taken as a signal of higher quality, while in fact it signals lower sustainability. From the sustainability labeling literature, there is strong evidence that color- coded gradient labeling at the point-of-sale is effective at guiding consumer choices (Piracci et al., 2024; Thøgersen et al., 2024). Therefore, we propose that it is pos- sible to reduce the ambiguity of true price information by combining it with color- coded sustainability labeling. In specific, we investigate the effect of different price presentation formats on consumers’ choices accounting for consumers’ price-qual- ity schema and understanding of true pricing. We extend the literature on price Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 Page 3 of 15 1 premium communication as well as provide managerial advice on how to communi- cate true prices to consumers. 2 Theoretical background 2.1 Numeric information processing at the point of sale Consumers are exposed to plenty of numeric information when conducting their shopping trips. Not only information on regular and offer prices, but also informa- tion about opening hours, quantities, nutritional facts, time-dependent discounts, waiting times, and more are represented in numeric terms. Research shows that con- sumers struggle with navigating the wealth of numeric information in the shopping situation (Santana et al., 2020). Adding true price information about hidden costs, related to the environmental, health or social damage that the products cause on their way to the shelf, might add to the burden of navigating the supermarket jungle of digits. Especially in a grocery shopping situation, which is usually characterized by low involvement and time pressure, it will be a challenge for consumers to pro- cess and encode additional numeric information correctly. For true pricing to support consumers in making more sustainable choices at the point of sale, the information provided must at least be easy and fast to comprehend. Adding more numeric information should not play into consumers’ anxiety of deal- ing with numbers, but should allow them to make an informed choice, which they feel confident in. A meta-analysis by Krishna et al. (2002) found that when price discounts are presented in relative (vs absolute) terms, perceived savings increase, despite the computational burden of transforming relative savings to absolute sav- ings to understand the impact on the personal budget. Their findings suggest that consumers do not actually compute the price impact on their budget but instead rely on the relative discount as an indicator of a good deal. This is in line with other established findings on consumers’ price knowledge (Vanhuele & Drèze, 2002). However, retailers rarely want to communicate price premiums to consumers, so it is uncertain whether relative or absolute price premium presentation formats will be more effective for communicating true cost. The literature on price premiums generally suggests that premiums are perceived as unfair, but that transparent cost information can enhance perceived fairness (Bolton & Alba, 2006; Bolton et al., 2003). The literature further establishes that it is important for companies to con- sider consumers’ price fairness perceptions and that fairness perceptions depend on the reason for price premiums (Kahneman et al., 1986a, 1986b). However, so far, the literature does not provide an account of the ideal presentation format for price premiums, in general or for TCA. Evidence from the existing market trials at Penny or Albert Heijn suggests that when hidden costs are communicated as absolute price premiums, it increases consumers’ focus on the overall true price and the sense that products are generally becoming more expensive (Stein et al., 2024). In line with this notion and building on the pricing literature on discounts, we suggest that when hidden cost are communicated in relative terms, their magnitude will serve as an indicator of sustainability. We further assume that consumers will use this indicator 1 Page 4 of 15 Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 of sustainability to guide their choices, and not to actually compute the absolute value of the hidden costs. We therefore hypothesize: Hypothesis 1: Presenting hidden costs in relative terms, compared to presenting them in absolute terms, will reduce the importance of price while increasing the importance of sustainability attributes. 2.2 Sustainability labeling as a tool to guide consumer choices The sustainability of a product, measured in terms of hidden environmental, health, or social costs, cannot be verified directly by consumers. Sustainability is there- fore a credence attribute (Darby & Karni, 1973), which can be communicated through product labeling (Fernqvist & Ekelund, 2014). If consumers find this labe- ling information credible, they can use the label to guide their choices. Consum- ers have learned to rely on different standardized labeling schemes related to nutri- tion (Ikonen et al., 2020) or aspects of sustainability (Asioli et al., 2020; Thøgersen, 2025). The most common and successful sustainability labeling in the food area is organic labeling, but there are plenty of different labels and new ones have been introduced in recent years, not least carbon footprint labeling. Consumers generally perceive sustainability labeling favorably and are willing to accept premiums for sustainability-labeled products (Piracci et al., 2024). Multi-colored gradient labels have been found to be especially effective in visualizing the degree of sustainabil- ity (Thøgersen et al., 2024), but other ways of communicating relevant sustainabil- ity attributes also have an effect, such as organic labeling or price information (De Bauw et al., 2022). So far, sustainability labeling has not been combined with true pricing paradigms, neither in research nor in practice. We argue that color-coded gradient labeling is a useful means to make it easier for consumers to encode numeric information about the hidden costs. A color-coded gradient label might even make numeric hidden cost information redundant. Based on the experience from sustainability labeling, it can be expected that replacing numeric hidden cost information with label information would reduce the cognitive load for consumers, leaving more cognitive capacity to process other product attributes and use them to assess the value of a given product. We therefore argue: Hypothesis 2: Providing sustainability information through labelling only (omit- ting hidden cost information) reduces the importance of prices compared to the combination of label and hidden cost information. 2.3 Old knowledge structures in new pricing paradigms Consumers are generally price-sensitive, so increasing prices for unsustainable products relative to more sustainable products creates an incentive for consumers to purchase more sustainably. However, price is also perceived as a quality indicator, where consumers generally assume that more expensive products are also of higher Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 Page 5 of 15 1 quality (Lichtenstein et al., 1993; Völckner & Hofmann, 2007). This relationship has been long-learned through repeated exposure to products and prices in the mar- ket and stored within existing knowledge structures in long-term memory. Updating these knowledge structures might demand more involvement than usually present in grocery shopping situations. Extending this challenge, the price-quality schema for sustainable purchases seems to be even more pronounced than for conventional products. Consumers have learned to expect sustainable products to be more expen- sive (Aschemann‐Witzel & Zielke, 2017). In addition, discounts on sustainable products have often shown less effective, probably because they interfere with key motives for sustainable purchase behavior (Feuß et al., 2022; Schwartz et al., 2020). However, implementing true pricing will lead to relatively higher price increases for unsustainable products than for sustainable products. This reversion of the pricing relationship for sustainable versus unsustainable products challenges learned knowl- edge structures regarding pricing and might reduce the understanding and effective- ness of true pricing. Findings from the nutrition labeling literature document that a good understand- ing of the provided product information is imperative for consumers to make correct inferences from the information (Meijer et al., 2021). Consumers with a high factual understanding of true pricing are likely to have updated their knowledge structures and will therefore rely less on price as a quality indicator under a true pricing para- digm. Hence, we hypothesize: Hypothesis 3: Consumers with a stronger price-quality schema will be less sensi- tive to true prices. Hypothesis 4: Consumers with a higher objective understanding of true pricing will be more sensitive to true prices. 3 Methodology 3.1 Sample and data collection The sample was collected by the market research agency SurveyEngine (https:// surve yengi ne. com/) based on an online questionnaire that contains a discrete choice experiment, among other things. To be able to control national idiosyncrasies and whether results are valid outside a single country, consumers in both Denmark (n = 673) and Netherlands (n = 778) were recruited for participation. For example, the Netherlands is a country that has had exposure to a true pricing campaign, while true pricing is largely unknown in Denmark. Another difference is that the focus on sustainability is relatively high in Denmark, for example reflected in the country topping the sustainable development goal (SDG) index (Sachs et al., 2019). National idiosyncrasies such as these might limit the generality of results based on samples from a single country only. The samples were representative in terms of age and gender. To be eligible to participate, respondents had to purchase ready-made pizza or ready-made soup at least occasionally. These processed food products were cho- sen as products which may naturally vary in their degree of sustainability, depending 1 Page 6 of 15 Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 on the ingredients and their value chain. They cover two standard categories in supermarkets in both countries, with varying sales shares (pizza higher compared to soup) to enhance the generalizability of the findings. 3.2 Discrete choice experiment and analysis A discrete choice experiment for ready-made pizza and ready-made soup constitutes the core of our consumer survey. Choice modelling allows for the elicitation of pref- erences following random utility theory (McFadden, 1974; Train, 2009), which has a long tradition in marketing research (Louviere & Woodworth, 1983). The method assumes that consumers trade off different attributes of alternatives in a choice set to choose the alternative which is expected to provide the highest utility. The theory assumes that we do not observe all of the utility in the choices, but that some utility remains unobserved (random). The observable component is captured by the attrib- ute levels that describe the choice options, while the error term captures the random utility component: U =V +𝜀 nit nit nit The utility (U) of an individual (n) choosing alternative i from a given choice set t is given by the utility of the observable component V nit = β´X nit and the random component 𝜀 nit . The utility of the observable component consists of a vector X nit describing the levels of the attributes of the i’th product alternative, and a vector of (unknown) preference parameters β. Following state-of-the-art procedures in the field (Lizin et al., 2022), we devel- oped a choice experiment with 50 choice sets consisting of three alternatives. For each choice set, the attribute levels of each alternative are based on an underlying experimental design. An experimental design describes the profiles (combinations of attribute levels) of all alternatives in each choice set. Instead of using random profiles, we adopted a more efficient design strategy that maximizes trade-offs across attributes in each choice set to capture more information about consumer preferences. Ngene (ChoiceMetrics, 2024) was used to generate so-called D-effi- cient designs, which minimize the D-error to capture maximum (Fisher) informa- tion (see e.g., Bliemer & Rose, 2024). Computation of the D-error requires best guesses for preference parameters β, referred to as priors. For the pilot study we assumed uninformative (zero) priors, whereas for the main study we considered normally distributed priors based on parameter estimates and standard errors from the pilot study. For each design we avoided choice sets with dominant alternatives (Bliemer et al., 2017). Each alternative varied in terms of a sustainability score on five levels (A = most sustainable to E = least sustainable), as well as the true prices (regular price plus a price premium based on the sustainability score: A = + 10% to E = + 90%). The regular price could vary on five levels from 2.99€ to 6.99€ with a one Euro increase in between levels (adapted to DKK for the Danish survey). Three presentation formats were considered for hidden costs, namely (i) presented as %-premium, (ii) presented as premium in absolute value, or (iii) not explicitly Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 Page 7 of 15 1 Note: Presentation formats in the pizza category exchanged the soup image with a pizza image Fig. 1 Illustration of presentation format conditions Fig. 2 Example of a choice set in the absolute premium condition for pizza stated. Organic or not was added as an additional product attribute to capture the importance of attributes other than price. An illustration of the different presentation formats can be seen in Fig. 1. Partici- pants were randomly allocated to one presentation format condition. For each prod- uct category, the participant was presented with eight randomly chosen choice sets, each consisting of three alternatives and a “none of these” option. For each choice set, they were asked to choose their most preferred alternative among the three alter- natives. An example of a choice set for pizza is depicted in Fig. 2. Those partici- pants who indicated that they did not consume one of the product categories did not see choice sets for this product category. For those participants who consumed both 1 Page 8 of 15 Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 products, the order of product categories was random to prevent order effects. Con- sumers who consumed neither were screened out. We estimated a latent class choice model with a known class distinction for pres- entation formats (i.e., experimental conditions) using LatentGold 6.0 (Vermunt & Magidson, 2021). This approach allows for a direct comparison of utility coeffi- cients between experimental conditions (Vermunt & Magidson, 2005). In addition, we assessed the interaction between the True Price parameter and consumers’ price- quality schema and their objective understanding of true pricing. Including these interaction effects allows an estimation of the change in utility when price-quality perceptions or objective understanding increases (Contini et al., 2023; Grebitus et al., 2013). The variables were mean-centered prior to analysis to ensure inter- pretability (Grebitus et al., 2013; Hayes, 2017). Whether or not the alternative was organic as well as the level of the sustainability score entered the model as a cat- egorical variable using effects coding. To ease interpretation, we collapsed the high- est (A + B) and lowest (D + E) sustainability scores to arrive at a three-level attrib- ute. The true price variable entered the model as a continuous variable. 3.2.1 Measures Objective understanding of true pricing was measured by five statements based on the consumer understanding model by Stancu et al. (2021) after exposure to infor- mation on true pricing, before the choice experiment. Consumers could indicate that the statement was true, false or that they did not know. Two of the five items were false. A score ranging from zero to five was created for each participant by summing up the correct answers to the five statements. Following Lichtenstein et al. (1993), consumers’ price quality schema was meas- ured based on the level of agreement with four items on a 7-point Likert scale after the choice experiment. The Cronbach’s alpha for the Danish sample was.84, for the Dutch sample.86. The items used to measure both constructs as well as the informa- tion text can be found in the appendix. 4 Results 4.1 Descriptive statistics Consumers’ objective understanding of true pricing was significantly higher in the Netherlands than in Denmark (M = 3.25 SD = 1.41; M = 2.58, SD = 1.57, NL DK t-value = 8.63, p <.001), probably due to the higher exposure to true pricing ini- tiatives in the Netherlands. The extent to which quality is inferred from the price was similar across countries (M = 4.33 SD = 1.36; M = 4.21, SD = 1.30, NL DK t-value = −1.7, p >.05). Of the total sample of Danish (Dutch) consumers, 36 (23) never consumed pizza, and therefore only made choices between soup alternatives, while 91 (171) Danish (Dutch) consumers never purchased ready-made soup, and therefore only made choices between pizza alternatives. Overall, the results in this table indicate that all chosen attributes are significant in consumers’ choices among pizza and soup products. A significant Wald statistic indicates significant differences across conditions. The findings further show that participants gain utility from organic labelling. This effect is stronger in the Danish sample, as could be expected from Danish consumers’ higher interest in sustainability (Sachs et al., 2019). Relative importances, calculated by dividing the maximum utility difference between the levels of one attribute by the sum of the maximum utility differences of all included attributes (Kallas et al., 2014; Vermunt & Magidson, 2005), are dis- played in Table 2. This transformation of the utility scores reflects the weight that the attribute receives in the decision-making process. As can be seen from Table 2, in both samples the (true) price generally is the most important attribute. The TCA concept reflects sustainability in monetary terms by considering all hidden costs, which occur in the value chain. For consumers to navigate this potentially new pricing paradigm, they need to understand why true prices are higher for some products and how this relates to the product’s level of sustainability. We contribute to the emerging literature specifically on true pricing and to the pricing literature in general by providing evidence that the absolute price pres- entation format, which has been employed in all practical tests of true pricing in retail settings until now, is less effective at promoting more sustainable choices compared to the relative price presentation format. Adding absolute numeric information about the hidden costs to the price information tends to reduce the importance of sustainability information and increase the importance of the price, even though price sensitivity did not differ across conditions. It appears that addi- tional numeric information increases the weight of this attribute in the decision- making process, apparently without adding much helpful information. This is in line with the findings of Santana et al. (2020). However, when hidden costs are instead presented in relative terms, the importance of sustainability information increases. Similar to research suggesting that relative price discounts serve as an indicator for a good deal (Krishna et al., 2002; Vanhuele & Drèze, 2002), in the case of true pricing information about hidden costs expressed in relative terms seems to serve as an indicator for the degree of sustainability. Yet, and in line with previous research on sustainability labeling (Thøgersen et al., 2024), providing true prices with a color-coded gradient label without addi- tional numeric information appears to be similarly effective at achieving this goal. In addition, by reducing the cognitive load of processing additional digits, this leaves more room for considering other potentially relevant product attributes in the consumer’s decision-making process, such as the organic label. Omitting true cost information might take away some of the fair-price justification, which has been found to be effective in validating higher true prices (Wilken et al., 2024). Nevertheless, this strategy represents an opportunity for manufacturers to guide attention to other relevant attributes, which are not price related. 1 Page 12 of 15 Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 We also show that there is a risk of misleading consumers into accepting higher true prices due to a long-learned expectation of a positive price-quality relationship. If consumers are not properly educated about the reasons for increasing true prices or when hidden costs are omitted, they might take the higher price as a quality signal instead of a signal of less sustainability. Since we observe differences in the strength of this effect across conditions, which are inconsistent across countries, this aspect deserves further attention in future research. It would be useful to better understand the price format signals that trigger an enhanced price-quality perception to tailor price communications accordingly (Völckner & Hofmann, 2007). In addition, we found that a higher factual understanding can counteract the misconceptions of the price quality schema, because a higher factual understanding leads to a higher price sensitivity also in the case of true prices. When information about hidden costs is missing, the overall true price might become a more prominent price signal, which especially consumers with a higher understanding of true pricing pick up. This could explain the stronger interaction effect in this condition. Yet, due to inconsist- encies across countries, the details of this mechanism deserve further research atten- tion. Future research could also consider investigating a scenario where manufactur- ers provide hidden cost information in different formats to see how this influences consumer responses. Important constraints on generality (Simons et al., 2017) of our research include the hypothetical nature of the survey-based research design, product category selection, and sampling. By using two products and collecting data from two countries, we can be sure that our key results are not idiosyncratic to a single product or country, but field studies in a supermarket setting encompassing whole shopping baskets and real purchases would enhance the external validity of findings like ours. 5.1 Managerial implication Implementing an all-encompassing true pricing regime will require a fundamental system change, which is beyond the reach of the marketing discipline. However, smaller initiatives, such as the Danish carbon tax (CNN, 2024), which imposes a price premium based on carbon emission equivalents at the producer level, are a step in that direction. This justifies our forward-looking approach of how to communi- cate such a price premium to consumers. Current market trials have highlighted the hidden costs of products in absolute money terms. Our results indicate that this pres- entation format increases attention to prices and is less cognitively accessible for consumers than alternative formats — while being less effective at guiding consum- ers to choose more sustainably. Better effects can be obtained by providing either only a color-coded gradient label communicating the level of sustainability of the product at the point of sale or by communicating the hidden costs in relative terms. Depending on which other attributes deserve attention, one or the other of these strategies might be preferable. To avoid misleading consumers to accept higher prices under the assump- tion that they indicate higher quality, which is not the case under a true pricing paradigm, true price labeling should in any case be accompanied by information Marketing Letters (2026) 37:1 Page 13 of 15 1 campaigns to raise consumer awareness and increase their factual understand- ing of true pricing. The focus of these campaigns should include the fairness and acceptance of higher true prices (Wilken et al., 2024), but also the level of sus- tainability of the product, using color-coded gradient labeling or other means. JSON: Name: true_pricing_presentation_dce Title: Discrete choice experiment assessment of the effect of price-presentation formats on consumer selection of sustainable grocery products under a true-pricing paradigm Short Hypothesis: Presenting product hidden costs as relative percentage premiums (versus absolute monetary premiums or no numeric hidden-cost information) increases the probability that consumers choose higher-sustainability grocery products. Related Work: Existing work examines (1) consumer numeric information processing at point of sale, showing that relative versus absolute price presentations differentially shape perceived savings and attention; (2) price-fairness and price-quality frameworks demonstrating that transparent cost disclosure can alter fairness perceptions but that consumers often use price as a quality cue; and (3) sustainability-labeling research showing color-coded gradient labels effectively communicate product sustainability. Prior true-pricing field trials and pilot studies have primarily reported absolute monetary premium presentations and documented media backlash and low willingness-to-pay; few studies experimentally compare presentation formats or combine numeric true-costs with graded sustainability labels. Limitations of current approaches include (a) a focus on absolute monetary disclosures without rigorous comparison to relative formats or label-only formats, (b) limited attention to interactions with consumers' price-quality schemas and factual understanding of true pricing, (c) predominantly single-country or single-category demonstrations restricting generalizability, and (d) sparse use of choice-modeling methods that estimate trade-offs and attribute importances across presentation formats. Abstract: This research pipeline proposes a controlled, cross-country discrete choice experiment to evaluate how three presentation formats for 'true price' information—relative percentage premiums, absolute monetary premiums, and label-only graded sustainability indicators—affect consumer selection of grocery products differing in sustainability. The methodology uses a D-efficient experimental design with multiple choice tasks per respondent, random assignment to presentation-format conditions, and choice-model estimation (latent-class and mixed-logit) to quantify attribute importances, marginal willingness-to-pay, and interactions with consumers' price-quality schemas and objective understanding of true pricing. The main contribution is a causal comparison of presentation formats that isolates whether relative representations or color-coded label-only displays more effectively shift choices toward higher-sustainability products while avoiding inadvertent quality-signaling of higher true prices. Expected outcomes include parameter estimates of presentation-format effects on sustainable choice shares and WTP, evidence on moderating roles of prior schemas and understanding, and prescriptive implications for point-of-sale communication design. Experiments: Dataset: online panel data collected in two countries: Denmark (n=673) and the Netherlands (n=778). Eligible respondents: consumers who purchase ready-made pizza or ready-made soup at least occasionally. Experimental design: D-efficient stated-preference design generating 50 profiles; each respondent completes 8 choice tasks; each task presents 3 product alternatives + opt-out. Attributes and levels: (a) regular price (five levels, e.g., 2.99–6.99 EUR equivalents), (b) sustainability score (5-level A–E, collapsed to 3 levels A+B, C, D+E for some analyses), (c) organic label (binary), (d) true-price premium presented in one of three between-subject conditions: (i) absolute monetary premium, (ii) relative percentage premium, (iii) no numeric premium (label-only). Treatment assignment: random, balanced across respondents. Sample targets: minimum ~400 respondents per treatment pooled across countries; per-country analyses retained. Baselines: absolute premium and no-numeric (label-only) conditions serve as baselines for pairwise comparisons to the relative-percent condition. Estimation and metrics: primary estimand is difference in probability of selecting high-sustainability alternatives between presentation formats. Model suite: latent-class choice model with known class for presentation format, mixed-logit (random parameters) for robustness, and conditional logit for baseline checks. Reported metrics: sustainable-choice share, attribute importance (normalized utility range), marginal WTP for sustainability, model fit (AIC/BIC), standard errors, and Wald tests for treatment contrasts. Interaction analyses: include interactions of true-price coefficient with (1) measured price-quality schema (continuous, mean-centered) and (2) objective understanding score (0–5); report marginal effects and significance. Ablations and robustness checks: (a) run models separately by product category (pizza vs soup), (b) omit organic attribute to test label substitution effects, (c) re-estimate using full five-level sustainability attribute, (d) test alternative coding of price (log-price vs linear), (e) bootstrap choice probabilities and WTP estimates, (f) test for dominance heuristics and remove dominated tasks, (g) test for order effects by randomizing product order. Statistical thresholds: two-sided tests with α=0.05; report effect sizes (Δ probability and Cohen's d where applicable). Pre-registration: preregister design matrix, primary hypothesis, sample size targets, and model specifications. Data release: anonymized choice data and code for replication. Risk Factors and Limitations: Hypothetical bias: stated-choice responses may not translate to real purchasing behavior; lack of real monetary consequences may under- or over-estimate treatment effects. Sample and selection bias: online panel respondents and country samples may not represent broader shopper populations; eligibility restriction to two product categories limits generalizability. External validity: lab/online DCE setting cannot capture full in-store attention dynamics, shelf context, promotions, or shopping-basket substitution effects. Attribute collinearity: sustainability scores, organic labels, and price premiums may be correlated and cause identification or multicollinearity issues in models. Measurement error: self-reported price-quality schema and objective-understanding measures may be noisy, attenuating interaction estimates. Cognitive-load confounds: unobserved differences in numeracy and time pressure could moderate treatment effects. Cultural heterogeneity: country-level institutional exposure to true-price campaigns may interact with treatments in ways not fully captured. Model risk: choice-model misspecification (incorrect distributional assumptions for random parameters or class structures) may bias WTP and importance estimates. Limited temporal scope: single-session measurement cannot capture learning or long-term behavior change after exposure to true-price formats. Regulatory and industry dynamics: retail implementation feasibility and label credibility depend on external factors not modeled here.
